Chapter 6 — When the Data Lies in Two Directions

Causal Analysis in Public Health Management | BK Advisors

Matthew Luke Kuch | BK Advisors

2026-04-18

Meet Hassan and Naomi

Hassan, 35, M&E lead at a Kenyan NGO (composite, drawn from county-level program reports)

Naomi, 38, district health analyst, Mwanza Region, Tanzania (composite, drawn from MOHCDGEC quarterly reviews)

They are comparing notes over WhatsApp on a Sunday evening.

Hassan’s NGO has just rolled out a free transport voucher for pregnant women in two Kenyan counties. He sends Naomi a graph showing delivery in a clinic is more common in households that received the voucher.

Naomi has been studying the same kind of programme in Mwanza for a year. She replies: “Look at the same data split by income.”

The question: When Hassan splits the data, the relationship flips. What just happened — and which version of the data should he believe?

And here is the puzzle

Aggregate (all households):

Voucher No voucher
Delivered in clinic 65 / 100 55 / 100

Voucher looks like it helps. +10 percentage points.

Same data, split by access to a clinic:

Voucher No voucher
Easy to reach 60 / 70 (86%) 45 / 50 (90%)
Hard to reach 5 / 30 (17%) 10 / 50 (20%)

In both access groups, voucher does worse than no voucher. But in the aggregate, voucher does better. Same data. Opposite story.

This has a name

Simpson’s Paradox

A pattern that holds in every subgroup can reverse when the subgroups are combined.

Simpson’s Paradox. Named for Edward Simpson, who described it in a famous 1951 paper. It is not really a paradox — it is a warning about what averaging hides.

And here is the unsettling part: the arithmetic is correct in both views. The numbers do not lie. The question is which view answers the question you actually care about.

Why the reversal happens

Look at the table again:

  • Most voucher recipients are in easy-to-reach areas. (70 out of 100 voucher households are easy-to-reach.)
  • Non-recipients are split evenly. (50 hard-to-reach, 50 easy.)
  • Easy-to-reach households deliver in clinics far more often anyway — even without any voucher.

The aggregate is comparing apples (mostly easy-to-reach voucher recipients) to oranges (a 50/50 mix of access). The access split takes the apples-and-oranges out of the comparison.

When to disaggregate

The picture decides

Whether to trust the aggregate or the split depends entirely on the picture.


Access to a clinic

⬇ ⬇

Voucher received Delivers in clinic

This is a fork — exactly the shape from Chapter 2. Access causes both whether you get the voucher (because the programme rolled out where there were already clinics that could redeem it) and whether you actually deliver in one.

When there is a fork, you have to disaggregate to remove the confounding. The split is right; the aggregate is wrong.

But sometimes the aggregate is right

Now imagine a different picture for the same data:


Voucher → Effective access (after voucher) → Delivers in clinic

If “access” is actually downstream of the voucher — say, the voucher includes a transport subsidy that creates access where there was none — then access is not a confounder. It is a mediator.

In this picture, disaggregating by access blocks the very effect you are trying to measure. The aggregate is right; the split is wrong.

Same data. Opposite advice.

  • Picture 1 (access → voucher and outcome): disaggregate. Trust the split.
  • Picture 2 (voucher → access → outcome): do not disaggregate. Trust the aggregate.

The data alone cannot tell you which picture is right. Only your causal picture from Chapters 2–3 can. Without the picture, “to disaggregate or not” is a coin toss.

The collider trap, in disguise

Why this connects to Chapter 5

Remember rule three from Chapter 5? “Conditioning on a collider creates fake correlations between things that are unrelated.”

Simpson’s Paradox is the flip side of that: conditioning on the wrong variable can also hide real causal effects, or reverse them.

The two errors come from the same source — adjusting for the wrong variable — and the same fix: draw the picture, then let the picture tell you what to adjust for.

Hassan’s resolution

Hassan looks at the picture. The voucher programme rolled out in counties that already had clinics — they had to, because the voucher could only be redeemed at a registered facility. So access is upstream of voucher receipt. It is a confounder, not a mediator.

He goes back to his board with the split numbers and a new sentence: “The voucher does not help. It looks like it does only because the programme reached the easy-to-access areas first — and those areas already had high clinic delivery rates without any voucher at all.”

That is a much more useful answer than “+10 percentage points.”

Three quiet warnings

Warning 1 — Always have a picture before splitting

Splitting data feels safer than aggregating. It is not. You can produce just as much nonsense by splitting on the wrong variable as by failing to split on the right one.

Warning 2 — More splits ≠ more truth

Once you have the right adjustment, stop splitting. Splitting further into smaller and smaller cells will eventually produce nonsense, because each cell has too few people in it (warning 2 from Chapter 4).

There is a sweet spot. The picture tells you where it is.

Warning 3 — Beware the “I disaggregated and the result changed” reflex

A reversed result is interesting. It is not automatically truer.

Whenever you split data and the answer flips, the very next thing to do is draw the picture and ask whether the variable you split on is a confounder or a mediator. If you cannot tell, get more interviews. Do not publish.

Try it yourself

You are the analyst

scenario

A national report says women who use mobile money are more likely to seek antenatal care.

Then someone splits the same data by region and finds that within every region, mobile money users are less likely to seek antenatal care.

Before you decide which version to publish: draw the picture. Where does “region” go on it? Is region a confounder or a mediator? What is the one piece of evidence that would settle it?

Hint: does region cause both mobile money use and ANC seeking — or does mobile money use determine which region you live in? The arrow direction is everything.

Looking ahead

In Chapter 7, we turn from “what is happening?” to “what should I do?”.

So far we have built pictures, put numbers on them, updated the numbers, and learned when to split and when not to. In Chapter 7 we use all of that to answer decision questions — which intervention, in which place, with what budget.

Further reading

The data behind the example

  • Simpson, E. H. (1951) — The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. The original paper. Surprisingly readable.
  • Pearl, J. (2014) — Comment: Understanding Simpson’s Paradox. American Statistician, 68(1). Open-access. The clearest modern treatment.
  • DHS Kenya 2014/15 + DHS Tanzania 2015/16 — for the underlying voucher / income / delivery patterns. dhsprogram.com.

If you want to go deeper

  • Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014) — Inference and Intervention. Routledge. Chapter 7 walks through the same paradox in a business setting.
  • Pearl, J. & Mackenzie, D. (2018) — The Book of Why. Chapter 6 contains the most accessible explanation of Simpson’s Paradox in print.

The one thing to remember

When data tells you opposite things at the aggregate and split levels, the data is not lying. The picture is what tells you which view to trust.

A picture with a fork → split. A picture with a mediator → don’t. Either way, the picture comes first.
